title: Senior's toolkit: finding your way in a cluster
summary: Contexts, namespaces, output formats and explain: the kubectl moves you make before touching anything.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: finding your way in a cluster
steps.body: Before you change anything, know which cluster and namespace you are in, then look at the objects in a form you can read.

toolkit.what: Lists every cluster you can talk to. The `*` marks the current one. Check it before any change: most bad days start in the wrong context.
flags: `kubectl config current-context` prints only the name
toolkit.when: every time you open a new terminal

toolkit.what: Switches the cluster that every later command talks to.
flags: on any command: use that cluster for one command only, without switching

toolkit.what: Sets the default namespace for the current context, so you can stop typing `-n shop`.
flags: change the context you are in now

toolkit.what: The list plus node, pod IP and readiness gates. The first view when something is wrong.
The full object as the API server stores it, including `status`. This is the truth, not the file you applied.
flags: `kind/name` lines to pipe into other commands

toolkit.what: A readable summary plus the recent **Events** at the bottom: why a pod is Pending, failing probes, pull errors.
flags: one pod; `describe pods -l app=api` for several
toolkit.when: a pod is not Running and Ready

toolkit.what: The built-in API reference for your cluster's version. Faster and more exact than searching the web for a field name.
flags: every nested field name in one tree
drill into one field with dots

toolkit.what: Every kind the cluster knows, with short names (`deploy`, `svc`, `cm`) and whether it is namespaced. Also shows CRDs that operators installed.
flags: include the verbs each kind supports

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it tells you.
pairs: which clusters you can reach, and which one is current
which node each pod runs on, and its IP
the stored object, including its status
a summary plus the recent events
what a field means and its type

steps.prompt: Make `shop` the default namespace of the context you are using now.
steps.explain: `set-context --current` edits the context you are in. `use-context` switches clusters; it does not set a namespace.

steps.prompt: You ran `kubectl delete deployment api` to clean up a test, and a minute later the production dashboard shows the API down. What should you have run first?
options: `kubectl config current-context` (or `get-contexts`) to see which cluster the command would hit
steps.explain: kubectl acts on the current context. Checking it, or passing `--context` explicitly on destructive commands, is the habit that prevents this incident. Many teams also show the context in their shell prompt.

steps.prompt: Your manifest sets `replicas: 3`, but you suspect someone scaled the deployment by hand. Which command shows what the cluster actually holds right now?
steps.explain: The API server's copy is the truth. Your file is only what you last asked for. `-o yaml` shows both `spec.replicas` and `status.readyReplicas`.

steps.prompt: Does the command read the cluster, or only change your local kubeconfig?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Open every session with `kubectl config get-contexts`, and put the context and namespace in your prompt. When something looks wrong, go `get -o wide`, then `describe`, then `get -o yaml`, and use `explain` instead of guessing field names.
